content.title: About
content.content: A gluten‑free cake or cupcake is baked using gluten‑free flours (rice, corn, buckwheat, etc.) and is often enriched with plant oils, eggs, and natural sweeteners. It is suitable for people with celiac disease, gluten sensitivity, or anyone seeking a lighter diet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gluten‑free baking gained mainstream popularity in the 1990s as awareness of celiac disease grew.
Xanthan gum or guar gum is frequently added to mimic the elasticity of gluten.
Combining several gluten‑free flours creates a more complex flavor and texture, closer to traditional cakes.
Many recipes incorporate applesauce or pumpkin puree to keep the crumb moist without extra fat.
Gluten‑free cupcakes can be easier to digest but may have a higher glycemic index if they contain a lot of sugar.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Gluten‑free grains such as buckwheat and quinoa provide a good amount of protein that supports tissue repair.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Adding plant oils (olive, coconut) supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Buckwheat and millet flours are high in B1, B2, and B3, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Xanthan gum and other soluble fibers in gluten‑free blends help maintain regular bowel movements.

items.title: Gluten‑free safety
items.content: Absence of gluten makes the product safe for those with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Allergy to specific ingredients
items.content: Gluten‑free baked goods may contain nuts, soy, or eggs, which are common allergens.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Some gluten‑free flours (rice, corn) can raise blood sugar quickly, so pair them with protein or fat.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Stabilizers like xanthan or guar gum are used for texture; excessive amounts may cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Even without gluten, cakes and cupcakes often contain significant sugar and fat, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the gluten‑free cake or cupcake as a dessert, topped with berry sauce, fresh fruit, or a dollop of low‑fat yogurt. It stores well sliced for quick snacks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cake or cupcake in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. Refrigerate for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze (wrapped in plastic and foil) for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Crackers, woven wheat are dry baked snacks made from whole‑grain wheat flour, water, salt and a small amount of vegetable oil. The dough is shaped into interlaced strips that are baked until golden, giving a crisp texture and a subtle nutty aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Woven wheat crackers have a long tradition in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines.
The weaving technique creates a distinctive pattern that promotes even baking.
Unlike many standard crackers, they often use whole‑grain flour, increasing fiber content.
They serve as a versatile base for cheese plates, pâtés, and vegetable toppings.
Variants may include sunflower or pumpkin seeds for extra flavor and nutrition.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat flour provides both soluble and insoluble fibers that support healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Thiamine, riboflavin and niacin in the crackers help maintain energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: These crackers contain little to no added sugar, making them suitable for moderate glucose control.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Wheat flour contributes a modest amount of protein that can complement other protein sources in the diet.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium and phosphorus are present, supporting bone health and metabolic functions.

items.title: Wheat/gluten allergy
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid these crackers.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Some versions are salted; choose unsalted varieties if you need to limit sodium.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although light, they still contribute calories; portion control is important for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy them as a snack on their own, spread with hummus, cream cheese, avocado, or use as a base for canapés topped with fish, ham, and vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store in the refrigerator to maintain crispness and prevent rancidity.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese, meat and dark‑green vegetables, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: A dish made from eggs prepared as an omelet or scrambled, enriched with cheese, pieces of meat (such as ham or bacon) and dark‑green vegetables (spinach, broccoli, kale). Added fat (vegetable or animal) increases the energy density.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs provide a complete source of protein containing all essential amino acids.
Dark‑green vegetables are rich in chlorophyll, giving them their deep colour and antioxidant properties.
Cheese contributes calcium and vitamin D, enhancing calcium absorption from the vegetables.
Fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E and K from the ingredients.
The meal is quick to prepare and is popular in breakfast and athletic nutrition plans.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat supply all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and meat provide B12, while green vegetables add folate, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: Meat and leafy greens deliver minerals important for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Cheese and dietary fat aid the absorption of calcium and vitamin D, promoting bone health.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Chlorophyll and vitamin E from vegetables and fat help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, cheese or dairy fat.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Using large amounts of butter or animal fat can make the dish high in saturated fats, which may be undesirable for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Salt and processed meat
items.content: Processed meats like bacon or sausage often contain high sodium and nitrates, which can raise blood pressure.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat the eggs with a splash of milk, stir in grated cheese, diced meat and finely chopped green vegetables. Heat fat in a skillet, pour in the mixture and cook to the desired consistency, stirring occasionally.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. Reheat in a pan or microwave, adding a little oil to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Jambolan (Syzygium cumini), also known as jamun, Java plum, or black plum, is a tropical fruit tree native to India and Southeast Asia. Its oval, glossy, dark purple-to-black berries have a sweet, tart, astringent flavor and stain the tongue and lips purple. Jambolan is eaten fresh and used in juices, jams, syrups, and desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The fruit turns the tongue and lips purple because of its anthocyanin pigments.
Jambolan is popular in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and across South and Southeast Asia, where it is a seasonal summer fruit.
The fruit has a single large seed, and the seeds are used in traditional practices.
The tree is long-lived and can grow very tall.
The fruit is often eaten with a pinch of salt or black salt to balance its astringency.

items.title: Contains anthocyanins
items.content: These plant pigments give jambolan its dark color and have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Provides vitamin C
items.content: Jambolan contains vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Provides iron and potassium
items.content: These minerals support oxygen transport and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Jambolan contributes fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Jambolan is relatively low in calories and refreshing.

items.title: Astringency
items.content: The tannins in jambolan can be astringent and may cause constipation or a dry mouth if eaten in large amounts.

items.title: Blood sugar medication
items.content: Jambolan, especially its seed and leaf extracts, may lower blood sugar. People taking diabetes medication should consult a healthcare professional before using concentrated products.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Jambolan allergy is uncommon but can occur.

items.title: Staining and seeds
items.content: The juice stains clothes and teeth, and the large seeds should not be swallowed in quantity or eaten by young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Jambolan can be washed and eaten fresh, sprinkled with a little salt, blended into juices and drinks, or cooked into jams, syrups, and desserts. Remove the large seed before eating. Eat ripe fruit, since unripe fruit is very astringent.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Jambolan is very perishable. Store it in the refrigerator and eat it within two to three days. Wash it just before eating. The pulp can be frozen for longer storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Peas and carrots cooked by boiling are a popular side dish and a staple in soups and stews. Peas are a legume rich in protein and fiber, while carrots are a root vegetable packed with beta‑carotene, vitamin A and antioxidants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peas belong to the legume family and are among the oldest cultivated crops used by humans.
Carrots were originally purple; the orange variety was developed in the 17th century in the Netherlands.
The pea‑carrot combination appears in traditional dishes worldwide, such as the British “pea and carrot mash” and the Russian “мутная каша”.
Boiling retains most of the vitamin C in peas, while heat improves the bioavailability of beta‑carotene in carrots.
Both vegetables are easy to grow in temperate climates; peas fix nitrogen in the soil, and carrots improve soil structure.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Cooked peas provide about 5 g of protein per 100 g, making them valuable for vegetarian diets.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Carrot beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, essential for vision and immune function.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Both vegetables supply soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting healthy digestion and cholesterol balance.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Vitamins C and E, along with carotenoids in carrots, help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Blood‑sugar regulation
items.content: Pea fiber slows glucose absorption, and the low glycemic index of the combo helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas, ranging from skin rash to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Peas contain phytates, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Possible pesticide residues
items.content: Non‑organic peas and carrots may carry pesticide residues; thorough washing before cooking is recommended.

items.title: Excess beta‑carotene
items.content: Very large intakes of carrots can cause carotenemia—a harmless yellowing of the skin.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve peas and carrots as a side dish, add them to soups, stews, salads, or casseroles. After boiling, they can be lightly sautéed for a crisp texture. Enjoy plain, lightly salted, or with a pat of butter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked peas and carrots in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags; they retain flavor and nutrients for up to 6 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Poke greens are a blend of leafy vegetables (commonly spinach, Swiss chard, kale and other greens) that have been steamed or blanched. The product has a tender texture, mild flavor, and retains most of its nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Poke greens are frequently used in Asian cuisine as a base for salads and side dishes.
The mix is usually prepared without added salt to preserve the natural taste of the vegetables.
Thermal processing retains over 90 % of vitamin C and almost all folate.
Leafy greens are rich in chlorophyll, giving the blend its bright green color.
The product is often packaged in vacuum‑sealed bags, extending shelf life.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for normal blood clotting and supports bone health.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is important for DNA synthesis and is especially beneficial for pregnant women.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Leafy vegetables are high in carotenoids and polyphenols, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber in the greens promotes regular bowel movements and supports gut microbiota.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 25 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If the vegetables are not thoroughly cleaned, pesticide traces may remain. Purchase from reputable suppliers.

items.title: Leafy‑vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to certain greens.

items.title: Oxidation after opening
items.content: Once the package is opened, the product can lose its bright color and nutritional quality quickly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Poke greens can be served as a side dish with meat, fish or tofu, added to soups, smoothies, rice or noodle dishes. They also work well in cold salads after a quick chill.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C in the original packaging. After opening, consume within 3–5 days. When frozen, the product retains quality for up to 2 months.

stewed-seasoned-ground-beef-mexican-styl.title: Stewed seasoned ground beef, Mexican style

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed seasoned ground beef in Mexican style is a ready‑to‑eat product made from 100 % beef, aromatic spices and a tomato‑based sauce. It delivers a rich, mildly spicy flavor with notes of cumin, paprika and chili, and a tender, juicy texture that works well in quick‑prep meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mexican‑style ground beef is a staple for tacos, burritos, nachos and chili con carne.
Slow stewing at low temperature preserves most of the meat’s nutrients.
Typical spice blend includes cumin, oregano, garlic and ground chili, traditional to Mexican cuisine.
The product can be refrigerated for up to 7 days or frozen for up to 3 months.
Stewed beef can be used as a base for vegetarian dishes when substituted with plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef provides a complete source of high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Stewed ground beef fits well into low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugars.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc from beef supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Seasonings can raise the salt level, so people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Bacterial risk
items.content: Improper storage may allow growth of pathogens such as Salmonella or E. coli.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Ground beef contains saturated fat; those with cardiovascular concerns should consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The stewed beef is ready to use: heat in a skillet or microwave for 2–3 minutes, then add to tacos, burritos, salads, soups, or use as a filling for peppers. It also pairs well with rice, beans or vegetables for a complete meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product refrigerated at +2…+4 °C in its original packaging for up to 7 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of ≥ 74 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: A turnover (or breakfast pocket) with egg is a ready‑to‑eat baked product consisting of a flaky pastry filled with an egg omelette, sometimes enriched with cheese, ham or vegetables. It is designed for a quick breakfast or snack, conveniently packaged and can be kept at room temperature for several days.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turnovers originated in Europe in the 19th century as a way to use leftover dough and fillings.
In Russia similar items are often called “breakfast pockets” and are sold in chain convenience stores.
The egg version is considered more nutritious because the egg provides a complete set of proteins and B‑vitamins.
The flaky pastry is usually made with butter, giving it a characteristic crunch and aroma.
Turnovers are frequently served in school cafeterias as a fast and filling breakfast.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The egg filling supplies high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain B12, riboflavin and niacin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Egg yolk provides heme iron, helping to prevent anemia.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Convenient
items.content: A ready‑made product saves time, delivering a nutritious breakfast without cooking.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to egg proteins and should avoid the product.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: The buttery pastry contains saturated fats, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Ready‑made items often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor portions.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: When stored at room temperature the product can spoil quickly, especially in warm conditions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The turnover can be eaten cold straight from the pack or warmed in a microwave (30‑60 seconds) or oven (180 °C for about 10 minutes). It is handy to take to work, school or on the go.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, consume within 2‑3 days or keep refrigerated at +4 °C.
